1. Detoxification in the Liver

The liver eliminates fat-soluble toxins and hormones in two phases.

PhaseEnzymesWhat happens
Phase ICytochrome P450 (CYP450)Oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, hydration, dehalogenation. Goal: less lipophilic. Caution: intermediates can be dangerous (free radicals, toxic metabolites)
Phase IIConjugation enzymesAdds a group to make it water-soluble: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione or amino acid conjugation. Excreted in bile/feces or urine
Detoxification: phase I and phase II (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Predict the disturbanceIf phase I produces toxic intermediates faster than phase II can conjugate them, or phase II is overwhelmed or deficient, toxins and reactive intermediates accumulate and damage the liver and other tissues.

2. Bile Salt Synthesis and Secretion

Route

  • Hepatocytes make bile salts → common hepatic duct → cystic duct (stored in the gallbladder) or common bile duct → duodenum through the sphincter of Oddi.
  • Function: emulsify fat and transport it (aid digestion and absorption).

Synthesis (from cholesterol)

StepWhereEnzymeProduct
1. Cholesterol → primary bile acidsLiver7α-hydroxylase (rate-limiting)Cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid
2. Primary → secondary bile acidsGut bacteria7α-dehydroxylaseDeoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid
3. Conjugation with glycine or taurineLiver (after return via the enterohepatic circulation)Bile salts: 4 acids × 2 conjugates = 8 different bile salts

Conjugation increases solubility at duodenal pH (so they stay ionized and work as emulsifiers).

Bile salt synthesis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Recycling and release

  • Reabsorbed in the ileum by the Na+/bile salt symporter (cholesterol is expensive to make).
  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) and the vagus nerve: contract the gallbladder and relax the sphincter of Oddi, releasing bile into the duodenum.

3. Fates of Bilirubin and Jaundice

StepWhereWhat happens
1Reticuloendothelial system (tissue macrophages)Red blood cell (RBC) → hemoglobin → biliverdin → unconjugated (free) bilirubin, released into blood and carried by albumin
2LiverAlbumin drops it off; UDP glucuronyl transferase makes conjugated bilirubin. Fates: (A) excreted in urine or (B) mixed into bile → duodenum
3Small intestine / colon (bacteria)Conjugated bilirubin → urobilinogen. About 5% is excreted in urine (some recycled through the liver); the excess → urobilin / stercobilin in feces
Fates of bilirubin (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Jaundice (bilirubin build-up; yellow skin and sclera)

TypeMechanismUrine urobilinogen
HemolyticMake too much (e.g., hemolytic anemia); excretion cannot keep up. Nothing is wrong with the pathway itselfPositive (urobilinogen present)
ObstructiveMake a normal amount but cannot excrete it (obstruction)Negative (absent)
Quick testA urinalysis for urobilinogen separates hemolytic from obstructive jaundice.

4. Glycogen Metabolism

Made in the liver and skeletal muscle. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase), so it cannot release free glucose; the liver can.

Free glucose →(hexokinase / glucokinase)→ G6P ↔(phosphoglucomutase)↔ G1P
SynthesisBreakdown (glycogenolysis)
Rate-limitingGlycogen synthase: makes α-1,4 chains from UDP-glucoseGlycogen phosphorylase: cleaves α-1,4 bonds, releases G1P
BranchingBranching enzyme: makes α-1,6 branches (only the branch point is 1,6; everything after is 1,4)Debranching enzyme: removes the α-1,6 branch, releasing free glucose
Stimulated byG6P; insulin (inactivates protein kinase A (PKA), activates protein phosphatase 1 (PP1))AMP; epinephrine/glucagon (GPCR → adenylyl cyclase (AC) → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase)
Inhibited byEpinephrine/glucagon (AC, cAMP, PKA phosphorylates and inhibits the synthase)ATP and G6P; insulin (inactivates PKA)
Glycogen metabolism (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
LogicFed (high glucose, insulin, G6P) → store glycogen. Fasting or stress (low glucose, glucagon/epinephrine, high AMP) → break down glycogen. In muscle, G6P stays in the cell (no G6Pase); in liver, G6Pase releases glucose.

Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)

TypeDefectNotes
I – Von GierkeGlucose-6-phosphatase (liver)Severe; cannot release free glucose
II – PompeLysosomal α-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase)Lysosomal glycogen degradation
III – CoriDebranching enzyme
IV – AndersenBranching enzyme
V – McArdleMuscle glycogen phosphorylaseMuscle only: exercise-induced symptoms, myoglobinuria

5. Gluconeogenesis

Occurs in the liver; makes glucose from non-sugar precursors. The brain and red blood cells (no mitochondria) depend on it. It is glycolysis in reverse except for three irreversible steps.

SubstrateSource
LactateAnaerobic metabolism; Cori cycle (lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) converts it back to pyruvate in the liver)
GlycerolTriglyceride hydrolysis by lipase (fat can become glucose)
Amino acids (mostly alanine)Alanine cycle: alanine aminotransferase converts alanine to pyruvate (α-ketoglutarate → glutamate)

Three bypass reactions

Glycolysis step (irreversible)Gluconeogenesis bypass
Glucose → G6P (hexokinase/glucokinase)G6P → glucose: glucose-6-phosphatase
F6P → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase-1)F1,6BP → F6P: fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
PEP → pyruvate (pyruvate kinase)Pyruvate → oxaloacetate (pyruvate carboxylase, in mitochondria) → PEP (PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK))
Gluconeogenesis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Regulation

Insulin (fed): inhibits gluconeogenesisGlucagon (fasting): activates gluconeogenesis
↑ fatty acid synthesis (less glycerol available); inhibits PEPCK↑ fatty acid oxidation (lipase releases glycerol); inhibits glycolysis and the TCA cycle (PKA inhibits pyruvate kinase and pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH))

Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are not run together (futile cycle). Marks' Table 28.1 lists the full regulation.

6. The Urea Cycle

Amino acid metabolism (transamination, glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), purine nucleotide cycle) makes toxic NH4+; the liver converts it to urea for excretion in urine.

Transamination and GDH

  • Almost every amino acid (not lysine, threonine) transfers its amino group to α-ketoglutarate, making glutamate and an α-keto acid. Aminotransferases need pyridoxal phosphate (PLP; vitamin B6).
  • Glutamate dehydrogenase then releases free NH4+ from glutamate (regenerating α-ketoglutarate).
#ReactionEnzymeWhere
1NH4+ + HCO3− (+ 2 ATP) → carbamoyl phosphateCPS I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I)Mitochondria
2Carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrullineOTC (ornithine transcarbamylase)
3Citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinateArgininosuccinate synthetaseCytosol
4Argininosuccinate → fumarate + arginineArgininosuccinate lyase
5Arginine → urea + ornithineArginase
The urea cycle (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

The two steps to know

  • CPS I (regulated step): activated by N-acetylglutamate (NAG), made when arginine accumulates. Feed-forward loop: more arginine → more NAG → more CPS I. Seen with a high-protein diet or a prolonged fast.
  • OTC: not regulated, but the most common urea cycle deficiency (X-linked). NH4+ builds up.
Clinical: ammonia toxicity / OTC deficiencyHyperammonemia affects the CNS: brain swelling (osmotic effects) and depletion of glutamate (a neurotransmitter) → lethargy, CNS depression, can be lethal. Treatment: low-protein diet (with adequate calories so the body is not fasting) and amino acid conjugates that are excreted, so nitrogen is used to rebuild those amino acids instead of making ammonium.

7. Cholesterol Synthesis

  • Uses: cell membranes; precursor of bile salts, steroid hormones, vitamin D. Sources: diet and liver synthesis (from acetyl CoA).
StepReaction
12 acetyl CoA → acetoacetyl CoA
2Acetoacetyl CoA + acetyl CoA → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase); 3 acetyl CoAs total
3HMG-CoA → mevalonate: HMG-CoA reductase = rate-limiting step
4Mevalonate → isoprene units (activated with phosphates) → squalene → ring closure → cholesterol
Cholesterol synthesis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Drug targetStatins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase (do not confuse with HMG-CoA synthase).

PathwayRate-limiting / key enzymeKey regulation
Bile salt synthesis7α-hydroxylase (liver)Gut bacteria 7α-dehydroxylase makes secondary acids; ileal Na+/bile salt symporter recycles
